evaluation.positioning_hook: A newly unemployed young man with a brain tumor falls for a woman only he can see, then risks everything to use experimental neurotech to bring her back for real.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediately legible and emotionally accessible: a love story, a medical crisis, and a reality-bending premise. The audience is narrower than a four-quadrant genre play because the movie lives in intimate, adult relationship territory rather than big spectacle.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands early and cleanly in the restaurant scene, then sharpens when Dr. Nakamura explains the tumor and Dr. Fisher frames the hallucination as a case study. The script keeps the central question simple: is Allie real, and what will Gavin sacrifice to keep her?

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Gavin is a strong lead because he is both emotionally open and self-protective, with a believable burden in Ruby and Thanh. Allie has a distinct voice and enough contradiction to feel like a real counterpart rather than a device, and Elaine adds a memorable supporting presence.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar romantic-drama setup and routes it through hallucination, memory, and brain science without losing emotional clarity. The repeated motif of things that are present but not fully real gives the piece a confident conceptual identity.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story moves with purpose once the hallucination reveal hits, and the adoption, tumor, and licensing threads keep adding pressure. Some middle passages lean on conversational repetition and emotional reiteration, but the stakes keep escalating toward surgery and the final memory twist.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script’s best idea is simple and sticky: a man falls in love with a woman his damaged brain may be inventing, then discovers the same mechanism can be used to recover memory and maybe love. That combination of romance, neuroscience, and grief feels novel while still instantly understandable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The L.A. geography, the adoption/legal backstory, the hospital system, and the startup research world all feel specific enough to generate story. The world is not sprawling, but it has enough institutional texture to support the plot and the emotional stakes.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct tonal blend of wry banter, melancholy romance, and speculative unease. Scenes like the bench meet-cute, the restaurant invisibility beat, and the final memory reveal give it a recognizable emotional register.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The script keeps revealing that the central relationship is also about grief, identity, parenthood, and the ethics of memory. The Allie/Ruby/Gavin triangle and the father-son thread inside Dr. Fisher suggest more emotional depth than the premise initially advertises.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Gavin-Allie dynamic is the engine, but the script also gives real weight to Ruby, Thanh, Elaine, and Dr. Fisher. It is not an ensemble in the broad sense, but the supporting relationships are active enough to generate recurring scenes and pressure.

lead_characters.name: Gavin
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid-20s, mixed race (one half Asian), working-age adult, recently unemployed, caregiver role thrust upon him.
lead_characters.hook: A sharp, self-aware young man who uses humor to cover panic, Gavin is trying to hold together a new life in Los Angeles while caring for his mother and a three-year-old girl he calls his sister. He is emotionally hungry but guarded, and the tumor diagnosis turns his private longing into a literal fight over what is real.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Andrew Garfield in The Social Network and The Eyes of Tammy Faye — fast, vulnerable, funny, and increasingly tragic, with a role that lets an actor play charm, denial, grief, and moral collapse in one arc.

lead_characters.name: Allie
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s, white, actress, East Coast transplant, emotionally intelligent but guarded.
lead_characters.hook: Allie is the movie’s romantic ideal and its most destabilizing variable: witty, observant, and self-protective, she seems to exist only in the spaces Gavin’s mind can reach. She carries real emotional weight even when the script is asking the audience to question whether she is a person, a projection, or both.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Natalie Portman in Garden State or Rooney Mara in The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo a chance to be enigmatic without being passive — a performance built on precision, chemistry, and the burden of being the story’s emotional ghost.

lead_characters.name: Ruby
lead_characters.hook: Ruby is the emotional truth test in the movie: a tiny child who can’t explain the legal or family mess around her, but whose presence forces every adult in the story to reveal what they actually value. She is quiet, observant, and unexpectedly funny in the way children often are when the adults are unraveling.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: For a child performer, this is the kind of role that recalls Jacob Tremblay in Room — minimal dialogue, maximum emotional impact, and the chance to anchor scenes through reaction, presence, and instinct.

lead_characters.name: Thanh
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 60s, Vietnamese, immigrant mother, grieving widow.
lead_characters.hook: Thanh is a woman who has spent decades surviving by shrinking herself, and the move to Los Angeles only makes her feel more invisible. Her resistance to the new life, and her eventual emotional honesty, give the film a second adult perspective on belonging, aging, and displacement.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-life emotional showcase that gave Youn Yuh-jung in Minari and Frances McDormand in Nomadland so much power — a role where stillness, pain, and dry humor do the heavy lifting.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Fisher
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 40s, white, psychologist/professor, intellectually driven, obsessive.
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Fisher starts as the polished expert who can translate Gavin’s experience into science, but the script keeps revealing that he is also personally compromised by grief and ambition. He is the bridge between the emotional story and the speculative premise, and that makes him quietly dangerous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong character-actor material in the vein of Paul Dano in Love & Mercy or Mark Ruffalo in Spotlight — a role that lets an actor play authority, empathy, and self-interest without ever becoming a villain.

lead_characters.name: Elaine
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 70s, white, retired state department worker, widow, cancer survivor.
lead_characters.hook: Elaine is the unexpected adult ally who sees through Gavin’s chaos and still chooses to help. She has the lived-in authority of someone who has outlasted several versions of herself, and her scenes give the movie its most grounded sense of worldly wisdom.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a delicious supporting turn in the vein of June Squibb in Nebraska or Blythe Danner in I’ll See You in My Dreams — a compact role with wit, authority, and a late-film emotional payoff.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Nakamura
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Nakamura is the blunt medical reality of the movie: calm, precise, and unwilling to indulge Gavin’s denial. She functions as the story’s credibility anchor, but also as a reminder that the emotional stakes are being measured against real physical risk.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of contained, high-authority role that gives an actor the crisp control of Regina King in If Beale Street Could Talk or Cherry Jones in Succession — efficient, intelligent, and scene-stealing without overplaying.

lead_characters.name: Samuel
lead_characters.hook: Samuel is the clean corporate face of the neurotech world, the guy who makes the science feel fundable and scalable. He’s not deeply explored, but he gives the startup thread a credible human intermediary.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a sleek supporting role for an actor who can play confidence and hidden agenda in a few scenes, similar to the function of a character like the tech-world operators in The Social Network.

lead_characters.name: Gregory
lead_characters.hook: Gregory is the legal reality check on Ruby’s immigration and adoption status. He’s the kind of practical supporting character who can turn exposition into pressure by making the stakes concrete and expensive.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is solid professional-character territory in the vein of a sharp legal supporting role from a prestige drama — the kind of part that rewards authority, timing, and clarity.

lead_characters.name: Cheryl
lead_characters.hook: Cheryl is a functional but useful hospital presence who helps keep the medical world tactile and human. She’s not a major engine, but she adds realism to the hospital stretch.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a concise, grounded supporting role for a character actor who can make institutional spaces feel lived-in.

lead_characters.name: Tara
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-20s, preschool teacher, warm, socially adept.
lead_characters.hook: Tara is the outside-world adult who briefly normalizes Ruby’s life and exposes the awkwardness of Gavin’s family structure. She’s a small role, but she sharpens the social stakes around Ruby’s care.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a clean, scene-specific supporting role that gives an actor a quick, memorable turn in a prestige indie.

Contained apartment and medical interiors balanced with recognizable city exteriors

technical.vfx_details: fMRI visualization, hallucination/perspective shifts, memory-flashforward transitions, and the final neurotech interface sequence require compositing and editorial effects rather than heavy spectacle.
technical.sfx_needs: Hospital equipment, practical medical setups, and a robotic implant device for the Synapulse sequence.

rights_flags.detail: Dr. Noel Fisher / UCLA professor reference is tied to a recognizable real-person identity and article-style depiction.
Barnes & Noble is prominently featured in the ending sequence.
UCLA is named repeatedly as an institutional setting and professional affiliation.
Synapulse is a named fictional tech company used as a central plot entity.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: adult prestige romance with speculative elements, best suited to streaming, specialty theatrical, or premium cable-style distribution.

budget.note: Contemporary Los Angeles with hospitals, multiple recognizable exterior locations, child casting, and moderate VFX keeps this above a simple contained indie but well below studio spectacle.

casting.note: The key lift is Gavin: he has to carry romantic charm, comic timing, grief, and escalating instability without losing audience trust. Allie also needs to play both specificity and ambiguity, because the final reveal depends on the performance landing cleanly.

development.note: The script’s central premise depends on the audience buying the Allie reveal, the tumor logic, and the memory-versus-imagination distinction; those are all clear on the page, but they are the pressure points buyers will interrogate.

comp_set.why_it_comps: A love story filtered through memory, loss, and the question of whether emotional truth survives altered perception.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who want an emotionally intelligent romance with a speculative hook and a strong grief component.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, skewing female but with meaningful male appeal through the sci-fi and psychological-thriller elements, college-educated, streaming-friendly audience.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary Los Angeles locations, a child performer, hospital interiors, and moderate effects keep this in the specialty indie lane rather than microbudget.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals dev execs building adult romance lanes
specialty distributors looking for elevated genre
indie producers with character-driven sci-fi taste
lane_fit.detail: The script sits naturally in the lane where emotional intimacy and a high-concept premise are sold together. It has enough genre architecture to market, but the real draw is the relationship drama and the performance opportunity.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed emotional arc; the premise is strongest as a one-off rather than a franchise or universe.

strengths.dimension_or_area: A romance built on epistemic uncertainty.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the movie a clean commercial engine: the audience is not just rooting for love, they are trying to solve whether love itself is being generated by damaged perception. That is attractive to buyers who want a date-night hook with real conversation value.
strengths.evidence: The restaurant invisibility beat, the hospital reveal, and the final memory-versus-imagination turn all keep the relationship under pressure from the same question.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Gavin is a real lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The part has enough humor, vulnerability, and moral compromise to attract a serious actor and give the project a face that can sell the movie. That matters because this is the kind of indie that can be packaged around one compelling performance.
strengths.evidence: His banter on the bench, his panic over Ruby, his denial about the surgery, and his final choice to pursue the memory tech all show a playable contradiction.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has a strong emotional triangle.
strengths.what_it_means: Gavin, Allie, and Ruby create a family-shaped pressure system that gives the story more than one emotional entry point. That broadens the appeal beyond pure romance and gives the movie a stronger audience aftertaste.
strengths.evidence: Ruby’s reactions change the temperature of scenes with Allie, and Gavin’s choices are repeatedly reframed by what Ruby needs.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world is specific without being expensive.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie feels rooted in recognizable Los Angeles and medical/startup spaces, which helps it feel premium without requiring tentpole spend. That is a useful positioning advantage for a buyer looking for elevated genre at indie scale.
strengths.evidence: Toluca Lake, The Grove, UCLA, the hospital, and the Synapulse lab all give the story a grounded, contemporary texture.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending recontextualizes the whole movie.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the script replay value and a strong word-of-mouth conversation point, which is especially valuable for a romance with speculative elements. Buyers like endings that make the audience immediately want to discuss what was real.
strengths.evidence: The final Barnes & Noble encounter and the missing tattoo force the audience to reinterpret the entire Allie experience.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige indie sci-fi romance with a clean, marketable hook and a lead role that can attract real talent. It combines contained production economics with a high-concept emotional premise, which is exactly the kind of package that can travel in streaming, specialty theatrical, or actor-driven financing conversations.

items.area: The Allie reveal is the whole buy.
items.detail: The movie’s commercial upside depends on the audience accepting that Allie is both emotionally real and neurologically unstable until the final turn. If that premise doesn’t land, the romance and the sci-fi engine both lose force, so this is the sharpest greenlight conversation on the page.

items.area: The middle repeats the same emotional question.
items.detail: Several stretches of the courtship and hospital material circle the same tension — is she real, how long do they have, what does he owe Ruby — without always adding a new dramatic turn. That makes the script feel more like a sustained mood piece than a relentlessly escalating feature for part of the second act.

items.area: The lead role narrows the casting pool.
items.detail: Gavin has to carry comedy, romantic chemistry, medical fear, and a destabilized point of view while staying sympathetic enough for the audience to follow him into the ending. That is a strong role, but it is not a broad one, and the project will likely need a very specific actor to make the premise feel inevitable.

items.area: The final memory logic is elegant but conditional.
items.detail: The ending depends on the audience tracking the difference between hallucination, memory, and recreated experience without getting lost in the mechanics of the tech. That is a satisfying twist on the page, but it is also the point where buyers will ask how cleanly the movie can communicate its rules.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest risk is that its most original idea is also its most fragile: the audience has to stay emotionally invested while the movie keeps asking them to question what they’re seeing. The cast lift is real, and the second-act repetition will be the other thing every buyer notices before saying yes.
